WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a Democratic initiative that would have taxed the windfall profits oil companies have enjoyed due to rising energy prices, with the minority leader calling the proposal a "gimmick." Record energy prices have led to record profits for oil companies. The measure failed to achieve the 60 votes required by Senate rules to proceed. The vote was 51-43. Six Republicans, including three seeking re-election in November, broke ranks to support the bill. Two Democrats -- Sen. Mary Landrieu of oil-producing state Louisiana and Majority Leader Harry Reid, who voted no to be able to bring the measure back to the floor under Senate rules -- voted against the measure. Along with placing a special tax of 25 percent on oil companies, the bill would have permitted lawsuits against the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, the oil-producing cartel, and suspended deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Profits from renewable energy sources would be excluded from the tax. "We're not afraid, on this side, to go after Big Oil when they are not doing the right thing," said Sen. Charles Schumer, D-New York. "And we are not afraid to go after OPEC because they are a cartel that squeezes us. "We're not afraid to do some strong tough things that will -- some in the short run, some in the longer run -- that will bring down the price, the all too high price, of gasoline." Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-North Dakota, said the measure was needed to "wring out" speculators he blamed for driving the price of crude oil to more than $130 a barrel in recent weeks . But Senate Republicans insisted the new taxes ultimately would hurt consumers and cut American oil supply, saying Democrats simply were playing election-year politics. The bill is "pure and simple a pathetic attempt to even call itself an energy plan," said Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said, "Hitting the gas companies might make for good campaign literature or evening news clips, but it won't address the problem. This bill isn't a serious response to gas prices. It is just a gimmick." The Kentucky Republican added, "They are hoping the idea of going after energy companies will create the illusion of action after a week in which they themselves fought for a bill that would make the problem worse. What a political charade." As the average cost of gas edged above $4 a gallon, high prices are definitely on the minds of voters. A CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll released Tuesday shows 40 percent of respondents are more concerned about the cost of gasoline than long lines at the pump, which occurred during the energy crisis of the 1970s. But 55 percent of those surveyed are more worried about the long lines and rationing. The poll results reflect telephone interviews with 1,035 adults on Wednesday and Thursday. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points. CNN's Ted Barrett, Lisa Desjardins, Matt Smith, Virginia Nicolaidis and Scott J. Anderson contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a Democratic initiative that would have taxed the windfall profits oil companies have reaped from rising energy prices, with the minority leader dismissing the proposal as a “gimmick.”

Record energy prices have generated record profits for oil companies. The measure fell short of the 60 votes required under Senate rules to advance, with a final vote of 51-43.

Six Republicans—including three seeking re-election in November—broke ranks to support the bill. Two Democrats voted against it: Sen. Mary Landrieu of oil-producing Louisiana and Majority Leader Harry Reid, who voted no so that, under Senate rules, he could bring the measure back to the floor.

In addition to imposing a special 25 percent tax on oil companies, the bill would have permitted lawsuits against the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, the oil-producing cartel, and suspended deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Profits from renewable energy sources would have been exempt from the tax.

“We’re not afraid, on this side, to go after Big Oil when they are not doing the right thing,” said Sen. Charles Schumer, D-New York. “And we are not afraid to go after OPEC because they are a cartel that squeezes us.

“We’re not afraid to do some strong, tough things—some in the short run, some in the longer run—that will bring down the all-too-high price of gasoline.”

Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-North Dakota, said the measure was needed to “wring out” speculators whom he blamed for driving crude oil prices above $130 a barrel in recent weeks.

Senate Republicans, however, insisted that the new taxes would ultimately hurt consumers and reduce the American oil supply, arguing that Democrats were merely engaging in election-year politics.

The bill is “pure and simple a pathetic attempt to even call itself an energy plan,” said Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas.

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said, “Hitting the gas companies might make for good campaign literature or evening news clips, but it won’t address the problem. This bill isn’t a serious response to gas prices. It is just a gimmick.”

The Kentucky Republican added, “They are hoping the idea of going after energy companies will create the illusion of action after a week in which they themselves fought for a bill that would make the problem worse. What a political charade.”

With the average cost of gasoline edging above $4 a gallon, high prices are clearly weighing on voters’ minds.

A CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll released Tuesday found that 40 percent of respondents were more concerned about the cost of gasoline than about long lines at the pump, which occurred during the energy crisis of the 1970s. However, 55 percent of those surveyed were more worried about long lines and rationing.

The poll results were based on telephone interviews with 1,035 adults conducted Wednesday and Thursday. The margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points.

CNN’s Ted Barrett, Lisa Desjardins, Matt Smith, Virginia Nicolaidis and Scott J. Anderson contributed to this report.

WASHINGTON (CNN) — Senate Republicans prevented a Democratic energy proposal from advancing Tuesday, dismissing it as political theater. The legislation sought to impose a 25 percent tax on oil-company windfall profits generated as climbing energy prices produced unprecedented industry earnings.

Under Senate procedure, the measure needed 60 votes to move forward. It received 51 votes in favor and 43 against. Six Republicans supported it, including three facing re-election in November.

Two Democrats opposed the proposal. Louisiana Sen. Mary Landrieu represents a major oil-producing state, while Majority Leader Harry Reid cast a “no” vote for procedural reasons, preserving his ability to bring the legislation before the Senate again.

In addition to the special tax on oil companies, the bill would have allowed legal action against the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, the cartel of oil-producing nations. It also called for temporarily halting contributions to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Income derived from renewable-energy operations would not have been subject to the tax.

New York Democratic Sen. Charles Schumer said his party was willing to confront large oil companies when they behaved improperly and to challenge OPEC over what he described as its efforts to pressure the United States. He argued that forceful short- and long-term measures could help reduce gasoline prices, which he said were far too high.

Sen. Byron Dorgan, a North Dakota Democrat, said the legislation was necessary to drive speculators from the market. He blamed such traders for helping push crude-oil prices above $130 per barrel in recent weeks.

Republicans countered that additional taxes would eventually be passed on to consumers and would reduce domestic oil supplies. They accused Democrats of promoting the measure primarily for political advantage during an election year.

Texas Republican Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison described the proposal as a wholly inadequate effort that scarcely deserved to be called an energy policy.

Minority Leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky said attacking gasoline companies might produce effective campaign material or television sound bites, but would not solve the underlying issue. He characterized the bill as an unserious response to fuel costs and merely a gimmick.

McConnell also accused Democrats of trying to appear active by targeting energy companies after spending the previous week supporting legislation that, in his view, would have aggravated the problem. He called the effort a political performance.

The vote came as the nationwide average gasoline price moved above $4 per gallon, making fuel costs a major concern among voters.

A CNN/Opinion Research Corp. survey released Tuesday found that 40 percent of respondents were more troubled by high gasoline prices than by the possibility of lengthy lines at filling stations, such as those experienced during the 1970s energy crisis. However, 55 percent said long waits and fuel rationing worried them more.

The survey was based on telephone interviews conducted Wednesday and Thursday with 1,035 adults. Its margin of error was plus or minus 3 percentage points.

CNN’s Ted Barrett, Lisa Desjardins, Matt Smith, Virginia Nicolaidis and Scott J. Anderson contributed to the report.

**Senate Republicans block Democratic oil windfall-profits tax bill amid record gas prices**

**Washington** — Senate Republicans blocked a Democratic proposal that would have imposed a 25% windfall-profits tax on major oil companies, halting an effort supporters said would discourage price gouging and provide relief to Americans facing record gasoline prices.

The bill failed to advance in the evenly divided Senate, where most legislation requires 60 votes to overcome procedural hurdles. Republicans opposed the measure, arguing that higher taxes on energy producers would discourage domestic production, tighten supplies and ultimately raise costs for consumers.

Democrats countered that oil companies have posted substantial profits while drivers are paying historically high prices at the pump. They said the tax would apply to extraordinary profits rather than routine earnings and was designed to prevent companies from benefiting excessively from market disruptions.

The vote underscored the sharp partisan divide over how Washington should respond to high energy costs. Democrats have focused on corporate profits, alleged price manipulation and clean-energy investments, while Republicans have blamed the Biden administration’s energy and environmental policies for constraining domestic production.

Oil companies have rejected accusations of price gouging, pointing instead to global crude prices, refinery capacity, supply-chain disruptions and geopolitical instability as key factors behind higher fuel costs.

With the legislation blocked, Democrats are expected to continue highlighting oil-industry profits as a campaign issue, while Republicans press for expanded drilling, fewer regulations and faster approval of energy infrastructure.

The measure’s defeat means the proposed 25% tax will not move forward unless Senate leaders bring it up again or attach similar provisions to other legislation.

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on the 51-43 Senate vote over the Democrats’ energy proposal, including its provisions, the lawmakers who broke party ranks, quotes from both parties, and recent polling about gas prices.
counterfactuals.output:
On June 10, 2008, the Senate voted 51–43 to advance the Democrats’ **Consumer-First Energy Act**, nine votes short of the 60 needed to overcome a Republican filibuster. Six senators did not vote.

### What the proposal would have done
The bill sought to:

- Impose a **25% windfall-profits tax** on major oil companies unless they invested more in renewable energy and expanded refinery capacity.
- Repeal roughly **$17 billion in oil-industry tax breaks over 10 years** and redirect much of the money toward renewable energy and energy efficiency.
- Give the federal government greater authority to act against **gasoline-price gouging**.
- Allow legal action against **OPEC members** for alleged price fixing.
- Increase transparency and regulation in energy-futures markets.

Supporters argued that the measure would make oil companies contribute more at a time when crude oil and gasoline prices—and industry profits—were at record levels. Opponents said the taxes could discourage domestic production and would not quickly reduce prices at the pump.

### Senators who crossed party lines
Five Republicans voted with the Democratic majority to invoke cloture:

- **Norm Coleman of Minnesota**
- **Susan Collins of Maine**
- **Chuck Grassley of Iowa**
- **Gordon Smith of Oregon**
- **Olympia Snowe of Maine**

**Mary Landrieu of Louisiana** was the only Democrat to vote against advancing the bill, reflecting the importance of oil and gas production to her state.

### Party arguments
Senate Majority Leader **Harry Reid** cast the vote as a choice between consumers and the petroleum industry, saying Republicans were protecting “**Big Oil**” while Americans struggled with record fuel costs. He described the major oil companies as the “**new robber barons**.”

Republicans countered that the legislation was political theater rather than an energy strategy. Senate Minority Leader **Mitch McConnell** argued that taxing producers would not generate more oil or lower pump prices, saying in substance that the answer to high prices was to increase supply rather than “**tax it and make it more expensive**.” Other Republican critics called the bill a “gimmick” and warned it could reduce investment in domestic production.

### Gas-price context and polling
The vote came as the nationwide average for regular gasoline moved above **$4 a gallon** for the first time. Contemporary surveys showed that fuel costs had become a major economic and political concern:

- Gallup polling found that roughly **six in ten Americans** said higher gasoline prices were causing their families financial hardship, with a substantial share describing that hardship as serious.
- An **ABC News/Washington Post** poll found an even broader impact—about **three-quarters of respondents** said gas prices were causing financial hardship.
- Polling also showed considerable public support for making oil companies pay more in taxes, although voters were divided over whether such taxes, expanded drilling, or conservation would be most effective in bringing prices down.

Thus, although the proposal won a simple Senate majority, it failed under the chamber’s 60-vote cloture requirement and did not proceed to a final vote.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a detailed political news story on the failed 2008 Senate measure targeting Big Oil and OPEC, explaining why it needed 60 votes and summarizing arguments from Schumer, Dorgan, Hutchison, and McConnell.
counterfactuals.output:
# Senate Blocks Democratic Drive to Tax Big Oil and Challenge OPEC

**WASHINGTON, June 10, 2008** — A Democratic election-year effort to penalize large oil companies, withdraw billions of dollars in industry tax benefits and give the federal government new authority to confront OPEC stalled in the Senate on Tuesday, as supporters fell nine votes short of the supermajority needed to overcome a Republican filibuster.

The Senate voted **51-43** to invoke cloture and advance the **Consumer-First Energy Act**, short of the required 60 votes. The result prevented the chamber from moving to full debate and a final up-or-down vote on the legislation.

The procedural defeat came as crude oil traded above $130 a barrel and the national average price of gasoline hovered around $4 a gallon, intensifying pressure on Congress to respond. Democrats portrayed the bill as a direct challenge to oil companies earning record profits and to the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries. Republicans said it relied on punitive taxes and political theater rather than measures that would increase domestic energy supplies.

## Why the bill needed 60 votes

The measure did not require 60 votes for ordinary passage. Under Senate rules, most legislation can pass with a simple majority once it reaches a final vote.

But Republicans opposed allowing the bill to proceed and could extend debate—a filibuster—unless the Senate invoked **cloture** under Rule XXII. Ending that obstruction required the support of three-fifths of all senators duly chosen and sworn, normally 60 in the 100-member Senate.

The 51-43 tally therefore was a vote to end debate on the motion to proceed, not a final vote on the substance of the bill. Although supporters had a majority of those voting, they lacked the supermajority necessary to clear the procedural barrier.

The distinction allowed Democrats to argue that a Senate majority favored taking up the legislation, while Republicans maintained that the bill’s sponsors had refused to build a broader energy compromise.

## What the proposal would have done

The Democratic package combined several approaches to rising fuel prices. Among its principal provisions, it would have:

- Imposed a windfall-profits tax on major oil companies, with opportunities to avoid or reduce the levy by investing in renewable and alternative energy;
- Repealed or limited tax benefits available to large oil and gas companies;
- Strengthened federal authority against gasoline price gouging;
- Increased oversight of energy-futures markets and speculation;
- Suspended additional purchases for the Strategic Petroleum Reserve while prices were exceptionally high; and
- Authorized the Justice Department to pursue antitrust action against OPEC members accused of coordinating production and prices.

The OPEC language reflected longstanding “No Oil Producing and Exporting Cartels,” or **NOPEC**, proposals. It sought to remove legal barriers that had made it difficult to sue foreign governments and state-owned producers under U.S. antitrust law.

The White House opposed the package and signaled that President George W. Bush would veto it. The administration and Senate Republicans argued that higher taxes would discourage exploration, refining and investment while doing little to reduce prices in the near term.

## Schumer: Consumers were trapped by concentrated power

Sen. **Charles Schumer of New York**, a member of the Democratic leadership, framed the dispute as a contest between motorists and two powerful forces: multinational oil companies and the OPEC cartel.

Schumer argued that the energy market was not functioning as a genuinely competitive free market because OPEC countries could restrict production while a relatively small number of large companies dominated major parts of the domestic oil business. In his view, record corporate earnings at a time of severe consumer pain justified withdrawing special tax treatment and strengthening antitrust enforcement.

He also contended that Republicans were protecting the industry while demanding more drilling as the answer to every price increase. New domestic production, he said, would take years to reach the market and would not provide immediate relief to families, truckers and small businesses.

For Schumer, the bill’s provisions on speculation, price gouging and OPEC were intended to show that Congress could attack multiple sources of high prices rather than simply granting producers greater access to federal lands and offshore areas.

## Dorgan: Record profits should finance a transition

Sen. **Byron Dorgan of North Dakota**, one of the measure’s chief Democratic advocates, focused on the contrast between oil-company profits and the tax advantages the industry continued to receive.

Dorgan argued that companies earning tens of billions of dollars did not need incentives from taxpayers. He said the proposed windfall-profits levy was designed not merely to punish success but to change investment behavior: companies could limit their exposure by putting more money into renewable fuels and alternative-energy development.

He also rejected the contention that the legislation represented conventional price controls. Democrats were not trying to dictate the lawful price of oil, Dorgan said; they were trying to recapture extraordinary profits, deter manipulation and redirect investment toward a less oil-dependent energy system.

On OPEC, Dorgan maintained that the United States should not treat coordinated production limits by sovereign oil exporters as untouchable when similar conduct by private companies would invite antitrust prosecution. He depicted the cartel as a central contributor to the transfer of wealth from American consumers to producing nations.

More broadly, Dorgan said the country could not drill its way to energy independence because the United States consumed a much larger share of the world’s oil than it controlled in proven reserves. Conservation, efficiency and alternative energy therefore had to be part of any durable response.

## Hutchison: New taxes would mean less domestic supply

Sen. **Kay Bailey Hutchison of Texas** offered one of the clearest Republican rebuttals. She argued that the proposal would make the underlying problem worse by raising the cost of producing and refining energy in the United States.

Hutchison said oil-company profits had to be viewed alongside the scale and risk of their investments. Exploration projects, refineries, pipelines and offshore platforms required billions of dollars and could take years to complete. Taking additional money from producers, she argued, would leave less capital available for those projects and could push investment to countries with more favorable tax treatment.

She also warned that describing the levy as a tax only on corporations obscured its likely effect. Companies could reduce investment, import more fuel or pass some costs along to consumers. In each case, she said, Americans could wind up more dependent on foreign oil rather than less.

Hutchison and other energy-state Republicans pressed for expanded access to domestic resources, including offshore areas and federal lands that were closed or restricted. In their account, Congress had spent years constraining supply and was now blaming producers for the predictable result.

Her argument was that the country could not “tax its way” to lower gasoline prices. A credible energy bill, she said, needed to promote production as well as conservation and alternatives.

## McConnell: A political exercise that would produce no oil

Senate Republican leader **Mitch McConnell of Kentucky** cast the bill as an election-year attempt to assign blame rather than increase supply.

McConnell emphasized that the package would not itself produce a barrel of oil, build a refinery or open a new area to exploration. He argued that Democrats were offering voters a list of villains—oil companies, speculators and OPEC—while resisting Republican amendments to expand domestic production.

He also said the windfall-profits tax repeated a failed policy. Republicans frequently invoked the federal windfall-profit tax enacted in 1980, arguing that it reduced domestic output and increased reliance on imported oil before being repealed in 1988. Democrats disputed the comparison, noting differences in the 2008 proposal and its investment provisions.

McConnell maintained that the bill had been constructed to create a campaign issue: Democrats could force a vote, accuse Republicans of siding with oil companies and then use the failed cloture tally in November. A serious bipartisan package, he argued, would combine conservation and alternative energy with more drilling, expanded refining capacity, nuclear power and development of domestic resources.

He also objected to moving forward without assurances that Republicans would be able to offer production-related amendments. That procedural fight became inseparable from the policy dispute, with Democrats saying Republicans were using amendment demands to block action and Republicans saying Democrats were trying to prevent consideration of supply measures.

## Majority support, but no path to passage

The vote illustrated the peculiar arithmetic of the Senate. Democrats could claim that more senators voted to advance the legislation than to block it, but majority support was insufficient in the face of a filibuster.

The measure also faced difficulty beyond the Senate. Even if Democrats had found the additional nine votes to invoke cloture and then passed the bill, they would have confronted a presidential veto and the much higher two-thirds threshold needed to override it.

The failed vote left both parties with sharply different political messages. Democrats said Republicans had protected profitable oil companies and an international cartel while motorists paid record prices. Republicans said Democrats had chosen taxes and lawsuits over domestic production.

What the Senate did not produce was immediate relief at the pump. The chamber’s vote ended the bill’s momentum without resolving the larger argument that would dominate the 2008 energy debate: whether Washington should respond to high prices principally by disciplining producers and traders, or by expanding the supply of American energy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a Washington-dateline article describing the partisan debate over high energy prices, oil-company profits, speculation, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and whether taxing producers would help consumers.
counterfactuals.output:
**WASHINGTON —** High energy prices are fueling a familiar partisan fight in Washington, with Democrats accusing oil companies and financial speculators of profiting at consumers’ expense and Republicans blaming federal policies that they say discourage domestic production.

Democrats argue that major petroleum producers have benefited from elevated crude prices while motorists and households struggle with higher costs for gasoline, diesel, heating and electricity. They have pointed to oil-company earnings, stock buybacks and dividend payments as evidence that the industry has had little incentive to quickly expand supply or lower prices.

Some Democrats have proposed imposing a windfall-profits tax on large producers, potentially using the revenue to provide rebates or other assistance to consumers. Supporters say such a levy could discourage companies from taking excessive profits during a period of economic strain and return some of those gains to the public.

Republicans and industry representatives counter that taxing producers would reduce the money available for drilling, refining and infrastructure, ultimately tightening supply and pushing prices higher. They say energy markets are shaped by global demand, geopolitical disruptions, refinery capacity and years of investment decisions—not simply by the pricing choices of individual companies.

The parties are also divided over the role of commodity-market speculation. Democratic lawmakers have called for greater scrutiny of traders, arguing that excessive speculation in oil futures can amplify price swings beyond what physical supply and demand justify. Republicans generally contend that futures markets help producers and consumers manage risk and that restricting trading would do little to address the underlying shortage of energy supplies.

Economists remain divided over how much financial trading affects prices over sustained periods. Speculation can intensify short-term volatility, many analysts say, but long-lasting increases typically require broader market pressures, such as stronger demand, constrained production or disruptions to transportation and refining.

The Strategic Petroleum Reserve has become another focal point. Administrations of both parties have used or considered using the emergency stockpile to cushion supply disruptions. Democrats say releasing crude from the reserve can provide near-term relief and signal that the government will act against severe price spikes.

Republicans argue that the reserve was created for national emergencies, not routine price management, and that repeated withdrawals can weaken energy security while offering only temporary relief. Because reserve releases do not add permanent production or refining capacity, their effect on prices is generally limited by the size and duration of the release and by conditions in the global market.

At the center of the dispute is whether higher taxes on producers would help consumers. A windfall tax paired with direct rebates could offset some household costs, supporters say. But the tax itself would not necessarily reduce the price of oil, which is traded globally. Depending on how it is structured, companies could absorb the levy, pass along part of the cost, reduce investment or shift production elsewhere.

Republicans favor expanding access to federal lands and waters, accelerating permits for pipelines and export facilities, and easing regulations. Democrats say additional drilling would take time to affect prices and advocate a broader strategy that includes short-term consumer relief, stronger oversight and faster investment in renewable energy, efficiency and electric vehicles.

The debate leaves policymakers confronting an uncomfortable reality: The measures most likely to provide immediate relief may have only modest or temporary effects, while policies capable of changing the country’s energy system could take years to influence household bills.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

## Senate blocks windfall-profits tax as gasoline tops $4 a gallon

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** — Senate Republicans blocked legislation Tuesday that would have imposed a windfall-profits tax on major oil companies, as the nationwide average price of regular gasoline remained above $4 a gallon.

The Consumer-First Energy Act fell nine votes short of the 60 needed to advance, with senators voting 51-43 to end debate.

The Democratic-backed measure would have levied a 25% tax on “unreasonable” profits earned by the five largest U.S. oil companies unless they increased investments in renewable energy and expanded refining capacity. It also would have rolled back billions of dollars in oil-industry tax breaks and strengthened federal authority to combat price gouging.

Democrats argued that record industry earnings warranted congressional action.

“Americans are paying more at the pump while oil companies are making record profits,” supporters said during the debate.

Republicans countered that raising taxes on producers would discourage domestic exploration, reduce supplies and ultimately push prices still higher. They urged Congress to open more federal land and offshore areas to drilling.

The vote came after the national average for regular gasoline crossed the once-unthinkable $4-a-gallon threshold, according to AAA. Diesel prices were even higher, adding to transportation costs throughout the economy.

A CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll suggested that Americans were considerably more worried about being unable to afford gasoline than about reliving the shortages and long filling-station lines of the 1970s. Roughly three-quarters of those questioned identified rising prices as the greater concern, while a much smaller share said they were more afraid gasoline would become unavailable.

The findings underscore how the current energy crisis differs from the oil shocks of a generation ago: For most consumers, gasoline remains available, but increasingly difficult to fit into household budgets.

With the windfall-profits proposal stalled, Congress remained divided over whether the answer was higher taxes on oil-company earnings, expanded domestic production, greater conservation or accelerated investment in alternative energy.
